transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I came in because I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I've missed something critical. It's like my brain gets stuck. I'll think I put a wrong number in a data release at work, or left the back door unlocked, or paid a bill from the wrong account. And the thing is, even when I know I checked it, my mind just won't let go of the possibility that I've caused some kind of disaster. It's getting really hard to deal with.

When you have one of these thoughts, like worrying you left the door unlocked, do you feel driven to do something about it—like go back and check, ask someone to confirm, or repeat an action—before you can feel okay again?

Yes, exactly. I have to do something to calm myself down. I end up reopening spreadsheets I've already closed, or rereading emails line by line. With things like the locks or payment confirmations, I check them over and over again. I actually have to do it in a set order until it finally feels, you know, safe to me. 

It takes up so much time. Some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours later doing this, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished.

latest_inference.note: The patient describes classic obsession-compulsion cycle: intrusive, unwanted thoughts causing distress, followed by repetitive, ritualized checking behaviors performed in a specific order to reduce anxiety, consuming hours of time. This pattern of ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts paired with compulsive behaviors aimed at neutralizing distress is diagnostic of OCD (F42) rather than generalized anxiety (F41.1), which lacks the compulsive ritual component, or obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (F60.5), which involves pervasive perfectionism/rigidity as personality traits rather than discrete obsessions and compulsions.
